newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sumitomo chairman resigns over copper loss.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo chairman resigns over copper loss.

text.p: The chairman of scandal-tainted Sumitomo Corp resigned on Wednesday and was made a special adviser to the trading house in a symbolic gesture to atone for its $2.6 billion in copper trading losses.

Two other members of Sumitomo's board of directors also offered to resign, but the Japanese company reiterated that its management knew nothing of the unauthorised deals by former copper trading chief Yasuo Hamanaka that generated the losses, the largest ever in a financial market.

Hamanaka, who was fired after confessing his secret deals to his bosses last June, pleaded guilty in a Tokyo court last week to charges of fraud and forgery in connection with the losses. He was released on bail on Monday but will return to court next month when his trial resumes.

Sumitomo said Tomiichi Akiyama, who was the company's president when it announced its losses but became chairman a few weeks later in a previously scheduled move, resigned "in order to put the matter behind (us)".

"While I knew nothing about Mr Hamanaka's hidden trading, I was the president of the corporation when much of the trading occurred," Akiyama said in a letter to Sumitomo's New York lawyers that was made public by the trading house.
He said he considered resigning immediately after the announcement, but remained in office to help deal with the aftermath of the scandal.
Sumitomo did not way whether the other two board members who had offered to step down, one of whom was Hamanaka's direct supervisor when he revealed his massive losses, would actually do so.
Japanese executives often resign in a symbolic gesture to "take responsibility" for any scandal or corporate embarrassment without admitting any personal or legal culpability.
Akiyama also said Sumitomo had responded in a model fashion to the scandal by bringing in outside lawyers and accountants to help with internal investigations.

At a news conference to announce the resignation, Sumitomo president Kenji Miyahara said the company's probe of Hamanaka's trading would take several more months, delayed by the limited information available from internal Sumitomo documents alone.

He said, for example, that the company learned some facts on Hamanaka's activities for the first time from a Panorama documentary programme broadcast last week by the British Broadcasting Corporation.
He added that, prodded by the scandal, Sumitomo plans to set up an office of market risk management for all commodities in April.

Sumitomo's system of checks and controls is likely to come under close scrutiny when Hamanaka's trial continues on March 10. Hamanaka's lawyers have said they will seek to show that lax controls contributed to the trade house's losses.
Miyahara reiterated that the company continued to give its full cooperation to investigations of Hamanaka's copper trading by British and U.S. regulatory authorities.
Miyahara said Sumitomo had cut back its copper trading activity since Hamanaka's departure, although it had no intention of withdrawing from the copper market altogether.

Until his firing last June, Hamanaka was known in copper market circles as "Mr Five Percent" due to the great influence he wielded. He got the name as his trading team was believed to control five percent of world copper trading.
